title.narrative: Provision of life-saving WASH assistance to affected rural communities in Qansaxdheere to mitigate the impact of dry conditions and displacements.

description.narrative: ltpgtSomalia continues to endure one of the most complex and protracted humanitarian crises globally, driven by a convergence of climate-induced disasters, prolonged conflict, and systemic underdevelopment. According to the HNRP 2025 “it is determined that there are 9.1 million Somalis affected by the humanitarian crisis. 47% of the population are affected by conflict, floods, drought, outbreaks (AWD/Cholera, measles) and displacement that disrupt lives and livelihoods, resulting in humanitarian needs”.ltbrgtIrregular rainfall patterns, exacerbated by the climate crisis, have led to successive cycles of drought and flash floods—most recently influenced by La Niña events. These conditions have decimated pastoral and agricultural livelihoods, leaving households with minimal to no income and pushing families into a state of chronic food and water insecurity. ltbrgtHRNP “During October and November 2024, southern and central Somalia received only 30 to 45 per cent of average cumulative rainfall. 10 Reduced rainfall during the Deyr season (October to December), linked to La Niña conditions decreased local food production and availability".ltbrgtQansaxdheere district faces 15 years of siege, limited aid, and near-total collapse of health services, with severe shortages in staff and supplies. Schools are non-functional or lack gender-sensitive sanitation and clean water—essential for inclusive and dignified education, particularly for girls. Displacement has become a survival strategy. Families are abandoning their ancestral lands and livelihoods, seeking refuge in overcrowded and underserved internally displaced persons (IDP) camps in urban centers. These camps, however, offer little reprieve. They are marked by inadequate water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services. Open defecation is widespread, clean drinking water is virtually inaccessible, and hygiene kits are scarce. Contamination risks are extremely high, particularly in densely populated areas, elevating the threat of cholera, diarrhea, and other waterborne diseases. Forced evictions affected 154,000 IDPs in Somalia by November 2024, with 93% of all evictions occurring in urban areas of Banadir, Bay, and Wogooyi Galbeed (HRNP Report). Women and girls face heightened risks due to unsafe sanitation, lack of menstrual hygiene materials, and exposure to gender-based violence, including CRSV and forced marriages to Al-Shabaab. Poor waste management further increases health risks and environmental degradation in both rural and displaced communities.ltbrgtKAAH will provide inclusive and sustained WASH support in Qansaxdheere by rehabilitating the Howlaha-guud borehole to improve water pumping, storage, and distribution systems and the two boreholes will provide safe water supply for more than 5,000 vulnerable affected communities in Qansaxdhere district. A total of 70 gender-sensitive and accessible latrines will be constructed, including 12 specifically designed for persons with disabilities (PWDs). Additionally, 24 community cleanup campaigns and 24 hygiene promotion sessions will be conducted, reaching approximately 12,000 people. These sessions will be supported by the distribution of 1,000 hygiene kits to improve the well-being of the climatic shock affected communities. In this project, KAAH is planning to provide life-saving WASH services to 12,000 beneficiaries (5,400 women, ltbrgt1,800 girls, 1,440 Bs and 3,360 men) for climatic shock affected IDPs and vulnerable host communities with recognition of people with disabilities, minority groups, and female headed HHs. ltbrgtAll activities will adhere to SPHERE and WASH standards, with a strong focus on gender-based violence (GBV) prevention, disability inclusion, and protection.lt/pgt
